title: Va'etchanan: don't forget what you saw (Deuteronomy 4:9)
hookLine: take heed lest you forget, and make it known to your children

lines: THE ROOM, THE RADIO, THE WEATHER.
cards: Ask someone who lived through a big day where they were, and you may hear the room, the radio, the weather. Ask their grandchildren about the same day, and you may get a sentence from a textbook.
Memory thins as it travels. A few generations, and a day that changed a family can become a date nobody can quite place.
Moses is speaking to people who were children at Sinai, or not yet born, and he seems to know how this goes. So he stops in the middle of his speech and gives them a warning.

teach.b: The warning, in the old Jewish translation, begins: "Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently, lest thou forget." Forget what? The things your eyes saw.
He means Sinai: the day you stood before God at Horeb, the mountain burning, the voice out of the fire.
And the verse goes on: don't let them slip from your heart all the days of your life, but make them known to your children and your children's children. Notice the order. First, guard yourself.
Take heed. In Hebrew, hishamer lecha, watch yourself, be on guard. Memory isn't automatic; it's something you protect, like a flame in wind.
Then, pass it on. Not as a lecture.

As testimony: what your eyes saw. The medieval teacher Nachmanides, called the Ramban, read this verse as a full commandment, to never let the experience of Sinai leave your mind, and to tell it to every generation.

And there's a curious afterlife to the words keep thy soul diligently. Later teachers heard in them a duty to look after your own body and life too, so the verse about memory became a verse about health.
Both readings meet in the same place.
What you were given has to be guarded, or it's gone. Moses can't make his listeners' grandchildren remember Sinai.
He can only make sure his listeners don't forget, and tell it.

how: Some Jewish prayer books include a short list of things to remember daily, and the day of Sinai, drawn from Deuteronomy 4:9–10, is one of them; Nachmanides counts not forgetting Sinai as a commandment.

o: and I saw: Moses' view from the mountain
and I remembered: the portion's theme
and I pleaded: the portion's first word

games.q: inside the warning — tap the pairs.

s: Moses assumes the people will remember Sinai on their own
he warns them: take heed, lest thou forget.
the words keep thy soul diligently were later read as a duty to guard your health
a verse about memory became a verse about looking after your life.
the verse asks for memory to be passed to grandchildren
make them known to your children and your children's children.

games.q: you lived through something your grandchildren will only read about. what does the verse ask?
o: let the history books tell it.
guard it in yourself, then tell it to them.
games.why: take heed to thyself lest thou forget, then make it known to your children and your children's children.

practice: Let one moment come back that you never want to lose: a birth, a goodbye, a kindness, a moment that felt holy or just true. Don't explain it; see it, where you stood, what you heard, who was there.
Hold it until you could tell it the way your eyes saw it, so someone younger could hear it one day.

wordCard.voice: Va'etchanan. And I pleaded. The portion where Moses, after his own no, turns to guarding what his people saw.

orig.note: Hebrew: take heed to thyself, guard yourself. the opening of Moses' warning against forgetting.

carryVoice: Your line: don't forget what you saw. Memory is something you guard. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently, lest thou forget
